fields.title: New rules for blood donation for gay and bisexual men
fields.description: Starting Monday, April 20, 2026, all donors, regardless of gender, will be asked the same questions about sexual activity in the pre-donation questionnaire.
fields.content:
These changes are part of the Australian Red Cross's ongoing efforts to ensure access to donated blood while ensuring its safety.

This follows changes to the sexual activity rules for plasma donors, which came into effect in July 2025, allowing 3,000 new donors to make nearly 10,000 plasma donations to date.

Lifeblood CEO Steven Cornelissen AM said this is a significant milestone for blood donation in Australia.

Previous donor rules prevented many members of the LGBTQIA+ community from donating blood or platelets if they had had sexual relations within the past three months, Mr. Cornelissen said.

"These latest changes mean that many gay, bisexual, and transgender men in long-term monogamous relationships will be able to donate blood or platelets for the first time."

"We've been researching and working on this issue for some time, working with governments, LGBTQIA+ advocacy groups, and the general public, and we're delighted to welcome many new donors to our centers today to donate blood and platelets."

Mr. Cornelissen stated that patient safety will always be Lifeblood's top priority, and some people will still have to wait to donate blood.

fields.title: Includes prehospital transfusion data and expanded insight into donor participation and patient needs across America
fields.description: AmericaТs Blood Centers (ABC), in partnership with ADRP, has released the latest edition of the "U.S. Blood Donation Statistics and Public Messaging Guide." This major update provides journalists and policymakers with new data on prehospital blood transfusions, post-pandemic donor trends, and the growing involvement of younger and more diverse donor populations.
fields.content:
• New Emergency Data: For the first time, the guide includes national data on prehospital blood transfusions, highlighting the vital role of trauma care outside of hospital walls.
  • Shifting Demographics: Since 2021, there has been a notable increase in blood donations from younger donors and communities of color, alongside a decline in donor deferral rates.
  • The "3% Reality": While 62% of the U.S. population (212 million people) is eligible to donate, only 3% actually do so each year.
  • Usage Statistics: In 2023, 3.65 million patients received red blood cell transfusions. Over 25% of the total blood supply is dedicated to cancer care.
  • Critical Need: Because blood components like platelets expire in just 5–7 days, the report emphasizes the urgent need for consistent, regular volunteer donations to maintain the national supply.

fields.title: WHO Updates Global Guidelines to Ensure Maximum Blood Safety and Donor Health
fields.description: The World Health Organization reinforces strict eligibility criteria to protect both donors and recipients in global blood supply chains.
fields.content:
<h1>WHO Updates Global Guidelines to Ensure Maximum Blood Safety and Donor Health</h1>

<p><strong>GENEVA</strong> — The World Health Organization (WHO) has released its latest comprehensive report on blood safety, reinforcing the critical importance of strict eligibility criteria for voluntary non-remunerated blood donations. As the global demand for safe blood products continues to rise, these updated guidelines aim to harmonize standards across international borders, ensuring that every drop of blood collected is safe for both the donor and the recipient.</p>

<p>According to the <strong>Blood Chain</strong> network's mission, transparency and adherence to international standards are paramount. The WHO highlights that while millions of units are collected annually, the disparity in blood safety between high-income and low-income nations remains a significant challenge.</p>

<h2>Key Eligibility Requirements</h2>
<p>The updated framework reiterates the core physical requirements for potential donors to ensure their own safety during and after the donation process:</p>
<ul>
    <li><strong>Age Range:</strong> Donors should generally be between 18 and 65 years of age.</li>
    <li><strong>Weight:</strong> A minimum weight of 50 kg (110 lbs) is required to ensure the donor's body can safely tolerate the volume of blood removed.</li>
    <li><strong>General Health:</strong> Donors must be in good health at the time of donation, free from colds, flu, or other infections.</li>
</ul>

<h2>The Importance of the "Test" Section</h2>
<p>One of the major shifts in the new guidelines is the focus on pre-donation screening. This is where our <em>"Test: Find out if you are eligible"</em> feature becomes vital. By using automated screening based on WHO criteria, we can:</p>
<ol>
    <li>Reduce the number of "on-site" deferrals, saving time for medical staff.</li>
    <li>Identify potential health risks for the donor before they even reach the clinic.</li>
    <li>Maintain a higher quality of the global blood pool.</li>
</ol>

<blockquote>
    "Safe blood saves lives, but the safety of the donor is our first priority. By adhering to these global standards, we create a sustainable and trustworthy supply chain for everyone." 
    <br>— <em>WHO Department of Essential Health Technologies</em>
</blockquote>

<h2>Global Impact</h2>
<p>Currently, about 118.5 million blood donations are collected worldwide. However, 40% of these are collected in high-income countries, home to only 16% of the world’s population. The <strong>Blood Chain</strong> platform aims to bridge this gap by providing a standardized, digital approach to donor management and eligibility testing, aligned perfectly with these new WHO directives.</p>

<p><em>For more information on how you can contribute or to check your eligibility, please visit our <strong>Test</strong> section on the home page.</em></p>

fields.title: Advanced Screening Protocols: Why Your Eligibility Status Matters
fields.description: Understanding the rigorous testing process that every blood unit undergoes to safeguard the community
fields.content:
<h1>Advanced Screening Protocols: Why Your Eligibility Status Matters</h1>

<p>At <strong>Blood Chain</strong>, we believe that the foundation of a resilient healthcare system is a safe and reliable blood supply. Behind every successful transfusion lies a rigorous, multi-stage screening process designed to protect the community. This article explores why eligibility testing is not just a formality, but a life-saving necessity.</p>

<p><img alt="Laboratory blood testing" src="https://unsplash.com" style="float:right; height:200px; margin-left:15px; width:300px" />Every unit of blood donated through our network undergoes sophisticated laboratory analysis. However, the safety chain begins long before the needle even touches the donor's arm. It starts with the <strong>Eligibility Test</strong>.</p>

<h2>The Science of Safety: What Happens to Your Donation?</h2>
<p>Once a donation is collected, it is put through a battery of tests that are mandatory under international health regulations. These include:</p>
<ul>
    <li><strong>Infection Screening:</strong> Testing for transfusion-transmitted infections (TTIs) such as HIV-1/2, Hepatitis B and C, and Syphilis.</li>
    <li><strong>Blood Grouping:</strong> Precise determination of ABO and RhD groups to ensure compatibility.</li>
    <li><strong>Cross-Matching:</strong> Specialized testing to prevent adverse immune reactions in recipients.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Why "Temporary Deferral" is Part of the System</h2>
<p>Many potential donors are surprised to find they are temporarily ineligible to donate. At <strong>Blood Chain</strong>, we follow the WHO guidelines to manage these "deferrals." Common reasons include:</p>

<table border="1" cellpadding="10" cellspacing="0" style="width:100%">
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th scope="col">Reason for Deferral</th>
            <th scope="col">Typical Duration</th>
            <th scope="col">Reasoning</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>Recent Travel</td>
            <td>1 - 4 Months</td>
            <td>Risk of exposure to endemic diseases like Malaria or Zika.</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td>Medications</td>
            <td>Varies (1 day to 1 month)</td>
            <td>Certain drugs can affect the recipient (e.g., blood thinners).</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td>Minor Illness (Cold/Flu)</td>
            <td>Until 7 days post-symptom</td>
            <td>Ensuring the donor's immune system is fully recovered.</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

<h2>The Role of Digital Eligibility Tools</h2>
<p>To streamline this process, our <strong>"Find out if you are eligible"</strong> tool uses a smart algorithm to pre-screen donors. By answering a few simple questions based on WHO criteria, donors can:</p>
<ol>
    <li>Understand the current health requirements instantly.</li>
    <li>Avoid unnecessary trips to the donation center if they are currently deferred.</li>
    <li>Receive personalized advice on when they can return to donate.</li>
</ol>

<div style="background:#f9f9f9; border:1px solid #ccc; padding:15px; margin-top:20px;">
<h3>Expert Insight</h3>
<p><em>"Screening is the most effective barrier we have against the spread of infections through transfusion. By empowering donors with information before they arrive, we significantly increase the efficiency of the entire Blood Chain network."</em></p>
</div>

<p> </p>
